Lots of economists, on both the left and the right, are in favor of the former approach you described. Specifically, the idea is to make a guaranteed minimum income or a basic income available to all persons, so that the government ends up subsidizing the minimum cost of living instead of shifting the burden to businesses. The idea is that a "mincome" (guaranteed minimum income/negative income tax/basic income) would simplify bureaucracy, eliminate "poverty traps" (where welfare benefits suddenly end after a certain amount of income is earned, which disincentivizes welfare recipients from seeking slightly higher-paying jobs that would make them ineligible for valuable benefits) and give people more flexibility in the labor market and more ability to take time off to develop new skills. At the same time, eliminating the minimum wage would give businesses (especially small businesses) more flexibility in hiring; if a job's only worth $5 per hour to a business but they think someone would actually be willing to take it, they can offer it.

The basic income idea, at least, has been tested and had fairly positive results. They'd need to come as a pair, of course, but that's what's in the OP.
